prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and for its first experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: B008 is the clearest case on the shortlist of a simple, general mechanism: a time-reversal-symmetric band structure carries a Z2 invariant, and spin-orbit coupling then forces protected helical edge states. Kane and Mele wrote this down in a minimal model, and the classification generalised to three dimensions and to photonics, cold atoms and phononics. Molenkamp's group gave the decisive experiment with quantised edge conductance in HgTe/CdTe wells. The idea has been confirmed independently by transport, ARPES and STM, so it is mature and arguably overdue. Six of eight members ranked it in their top three, and all six proposed the same trio, which is unusual agreement on both merit and attribution. Theory first and experiment second is also the pattern the prize has honoured most reliably.
statement.case_against: The credited trio omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal is what made Molenkamp's experiment possible, and the 3D generalisation (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Roy; Hasan's ARPES) is also left out. Zhang died in 2018, which leaves the BHZ credit hard to represent in a three-person limit. The 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and phases of matter may lead some members to see this as a continuation. Finally, the protection of edge transport in real devices is subtler than the clean picture, and practical applications are still limited.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube discovery first as an instrument-driven opening of a new observational window, and he says he must lean heavily on colleagues for B008 because it is outside his expertise.
responses.response: I accept the weight on instrument-driven discoveries, and I also see that IceCube's diffuse flux is firmly confirmed. My reservation is attribution: a collaboration of hundreds and the AMANDA pioneers cannot be fairly captured by Halzen, Karle and Spiering, and several members already doubt the trio. B008 has a cleaner theory-plus-experiment split, with a minimal model and a decisive transport measurement. Where he defers, I would say that the topological case rests on checks from several independent probes, not on one measurement.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first, with Katori and Ye as a compact, defensible pair, mature and confirmed by many laboratories, with the second possibly to be redefined, and she puts B008 second.
responses.response: I agree that B035 is the best-attributed and most mature candidate on the list, and I keep it as a serious alternative. My difference with her is about what is new in principle. Katori's magic-wavelength idea is an elegant invention. But it sits next to the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, so the committee has already rewarded much of the metrology line. The Z2 classification created a new category of matter, which I weigh more. I would not oppose a combined prize, but the two do not belong together under one citation.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture behind essentially all superconducting processors, and he notes that the 2025 prize is close in subject and that he has ties to this community.
responses.response: I ranked B004 second and consider it very mature and well attributed as theory (Blais) plus experiments (Wallraff, Schoelkopf). I share his worry about the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits: the committee will have to explain why a second circuit prize is distinct, and Girvin and Devoret complicate the credit. Since he has flagged his own ties, I would weight his ranking carefully but not discount his physics. I find B004 a good candidate for a later year, with a gap after 2025, rather than for this year.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B008 first, calling the quantum spin Hall state a new quantum state of matter predicted by theory and seen in HgTe, and he flags BHZ as a known allocation problem; he ranks twisted bilayer graphene second.
responses.response: I agree, and I share his flag on BHZ. I would not use B051 as the second part of a shared prize. The mechanism for the superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene is still debated, the field is only about eight years old, and the credit has additional claimants (Cao, Fatemi and earlier twist-angle theory). The topological result is stable by comparison.

uncertainties: Whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be handled within a three-person limit, or whether the committee should instead phrase the citation around Kane, Mele and Molenkamp's decisive roles.
How much the 2016 prize should count against a second topological-matter prize.
Whether the committee prefers B035 on maturity and cleaner attribution over B008 on conceptual novelty.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of the credited candidates is a known co-author or institutional colleague. My field (stochastic and complex systems) is not condensed-matter topology, so my ranking rests on the conceptual argument.
